vision.name: Signal Yard
vision.tagline: One dock. Every agent. Every signal finds its place.
vision.description: Signal Yard is a unified ingestion and observability hub that acts as connective tissue between SOAR tooling, dev agents, PM systems, and human operators. Any agent can self-onboard and start shipping data immediately, even with previously unseen payload shapes. Unknown data is quarantined and classified by an AI agent, which proposes a schema patch for human review rather than silently mutating the ingestion contract or dropping data. It is MCP-native, OTel-standard, and built on proven observability infrastructure (Grafana/Loki/Tempo/Mimir/Postgres) with a single Go binary as its core spine.
goals: Provide a single place to view signal from SOAR alerts, dev agent traces, PM ticket updates, and other event sources
Enable any agent to self-onboard and begin sending data without hand-written ingestion pipelines
Automatically classify unknown data shapes via an AI classifier agent and propose schema patches
Keep humans in the loop with a reviewable approval workflow for all schema changes (human veto over AI proposals)
Support MCP-native agent discovery and tool usage alongside REST/OTLP/webhook ingestion
Build on standard, boring, proven observability infrastructure (OTel, Loki, Tempo, Mimir, Postgres, Grafana) rather than a bespoke storage format
Maintain a versioned, git-backed, auditable schema registry
target_users: Developers and dev-agent operators tracking agentic coding activity
Product/PM stakeholders tracking ticket velocity and PM system events
Executives needing a simple, jargon-free rollup view
AI agents and agent frameworks (MCP-native or REST/OTLP-based) that need to ship telemetry/events
vision.problem_statement: Signal is scattered across disparate tools (SOAR alerts, agentic coding traces, PM ticket systems, custom webhook events), with no single place for anyone to observe it holistically. Every new tool or agent with a novel payload shape requires a hand-written, bespoke ingestion pipeline, creating ongoing maintenance burden and blind spots.
success_metrics: Time from a new agent's first request to /start-here-agents to its first successfully ingested event
Number of unknown payload shapes successfully auto-classified and proposed as schema patches without manual coding
Percentage of schema proposals approved on first review vs. requiring rework
Reduction in engineering time spent building custom ingestion pipelines for new tools/agents
Latency of known-schema event ingestion (target: milliseconds)
Adoption rate of MCP-native onboarding vs. legacy REST/webhook onboarding
Volume/diversity of agent types successfully self-onboarded
Dashboard usage/engagement across SOAR, dev-agent, PM, and exec rollup views

frontend.design_notes:
Signal Yard's UI is the "human veto layer" for a machine-speed ingestion system — it should feel like a mission control deck crossed with a code-review tool, not a generic admin CRUD panel. Visual language: dark-mode-first, data-dense, terminal-adjacent (monospace for schema/JSON, sans for chrome), with a restrained accent palette — amber/green/red reserved specifically for signal-health states (known/quarantined/error) so status always pops against neutral slate backgrounds. Grafana is embedded (iframe panels via signed dashboard URLs) for time-series exploration; the custom React app owns everything Grafana can't: the Approval Queue (the star of the show), Agent Registry, Schema Registry diff/history, and Onboarding.

Layout: persistent left sidebar nav (collapsible, icon+label), top bar with global org/environment switcher, live event-rate sparkline, and a "Proposals awaiting review" badge that pulses when count > 0 — this is the single most important notification in the product since it represents the human bottleneck by design.

The centerpiece is the Schema Proposal Review screen: a two/three-pane diff view (raw quarantined payload → AI-proposed JSON Schema/YAML patch → resulting normalized event), rendered with a code-diff component (Monaco or shiki-based), Approve/Reject/Request-Changes actions, and inline comments. This should feel like reviewing a pull request, deliberately — because that's the mental model (git-backed schema registry, diffable, revertible). Treat every quarantine bucket item as a "PR" card with category guess, confidence score, sample count, and age.

Agent Registry is a card/table hybrid — each agent gets a "trust card" (name, key status, last-seen, event volume sparkline, categories it emits) so the security-minded owner can eyeball agent health without digging into Grafana.

Onboarding flow (/start-here-agents rendered for humans, not just machines) is a syntax-highlighted, copy-pasteable "agent starter kit" page — manifest viewer, curl examples, MCP tool list, API key generation wizard — because the product's growth loop depends on making self-onboarding feel trivially easy even for a human skimming docs before wiring up their agent.

Tone: confident, slightly playful copy in empty/success states ("Nothing in quarantine. Every signal found its place.") but deadly serious, high-contrast clarity in anything security/auth related (API keys, approval actions) — no cute copy near destructive or trust-sensitive actions.

Libraries: React + TypeScript + Vite, shadcn/ui + Tailwind for chrome, Radix primitives underneath, TanStack Query for all server state (aggressive use of polling/websocket invalidation for the live proposal queue and agent heartbeats), Zustand for local UI/session state (sidebar collapse, active org/env, draft comments, wizard step state), TanStack Table for registry/queue tables, Monaco Editor (or shiki + custom diff renderer) for schema/JSON diffing, react-hook-form + zod for all forms (register/login/api-key creation), recharts or visx for the small sparklines/heatmaps that aren't delegated to embedded Grafana, and an iframe wrapper component with signed-URL handling for embedded Grafana panels.
frontend.theme: shadcn/ui (dark-mode default) + tailwind, slate neutrals with amber/green/red semantic status accents, monospace (JetBrains Mono) for code/schema/JSON surfaces

clients.description: Client for the Go-based core API gateway: health/metrics, agent onboarding & registration, auth/session/API-key issuance, generic event collection, OTLP ingestion passthrough, and MCP tool endpoints. All methods throw `EventMeshApiError` on non-2xx responses with parsed error body; network failures throw the underlying fetch error wrapped as `EventMeshApiError` with status 0.

methods.name: health
methods.description: Check gateway liveness/readiness. Does not require auth. Returns quickly; use for uptime probes. Throws EventMeshApiError on 5xx.

methods.name: metrics
methods.description: Fetch raw Prometheus text-format metrics for the gateway. Returns the raw exposition text; caller is responsible for parsing. No auth required in typical deployments but may be gated at network layer.

methods.name: getStartHereManifest
methods.description: Fetch the self-onboarding manifest for agents, including capability manifest, schema URLs, MCP manifest link, and example payloads. Intended as the first call for any new agent integration; no auth required.

methods.name: registerAgent
methods.description: Register a new agent and request initial credentials. Returns a pending agent id; approval workflow happens out-of-band. Throws EventMeshApiError(409) if agent name already exists.

methods.name: login
methods.description: Exchange an OIDC credential/token for a dashboard session token. On success, pass returned sessionToken into client.setToken(). Throws EventMeshApiError(401) on invalid credentials.

methods.name: createApiKey
methods.description: Issue a new API key/JWT for an approved agent. Requires an authenticated session with sufficient privilege. The plaintext token is only returned once in this response; store securely.

methods.name: getApiKey
methods.description: Fetch metadata (not the secret) about an issued API key by id. Throws EventMeshApiError(404) if not found.

methods.name: revokeApiKey
methods.description: Revoke an API key immediately. Idempotent: calling on an already-revoked key returns success. Throws EventMeshApiError(404) if key never existed.

methods.name: collectEvent
methods.description: Generic JSON event intake (HEC-style token auth via optional hecToken option, falling back to the client's bearer token). Returns whether the event was accepted or quarantined for classification. Throws EventMeshApiError(400) on malformed payload.
methods.typescript_signature: async collectEvent(event: CollectEventRequest, options?: { hecToken?: string }): Promise<CollectEventResponse>

methods.name: ingestOtlpTraces
methods.description: OTLP traces ingestion passthrough. Accepts the raw OTLP JSON/protobuf-as-JSON body and forwards it downstream. Returns partial-success info if some spans were rejected.

methods.name: ingestOtlpMetrics
methods.description: OTLP metrics ingestion passthrough. Accepts raw OTLP metrics JSON and forwards downstream.

methods.name: ingestOtlpLogs
methods.description: OTLP logs ingestion passthrough. Accepts raw OTLP logs JSON and forwards downstream.

methods.name: mcpIngestEvent
methods.description: MCP tool endpoint: ingest an event via MCP protocol wrapper. Generic over the tool argument/result shape for strong typing at call sites.

sdk.auth_pattern: Bearer token (API key/JWT or dashboard session token) sent via `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. Tokens are held only in memory by the top-level `EventMeshClient` (never persisted to localStorage/cookies by the SDK itself) and injected into every outgoing request by a shared `fetch`-based HTTP core. `EventMeshClient.setToken(token: string)` / `.clearToken()` mutate the in-memory token; `login()` and `issueApiKey()` responses can be piped directly into `setToken()`. HEC-style ingestion (`/v1/collect`) and OTLP endpoints support a separate `X-HEC-Token` header via a per-call `hecToken` option for agents that don't have a full session. All client classes share one underlying `HttpCore` instance so token rotation is instant across services.
sdk.base_url_config: Single `baseUrl` passed to the `EventMeshClient` constructor (e.g. `https://api.eventmesh.example.com`), or via `EVENTMESH_BASE_URL` env var convention documented for server-side usage. Internally each per-service sub-client (gateway, normalizer, registry, classifier, webhook) is mounted on the same base URL since all services sit behind one gateway; an optional `basePathOverrides` map allows pointing individual services at different hosts for local dev/testing.

adrs.title: Use Go for all latency-sensitive core services; Python isolated to Classifier Agent
adrs.context: Signal Yard's core path (gateway, normalizer/router, schema registry, webhook adapters) needs to handle high-throughput, low-latency event ingestion and validation across many agent producers. The Classifier Agent's job is fundamentally different: it needs rich LLM SDK support (Anthropic/OpenAI/Ollama clients) and flexible prompt/response parsing, where Python's ecosystem is dominant. Splitting languages by workload profile avoids forcing either a slow hot-path or a painful LLM-orchestration story in Go.
adrs.decision: All services on the synchronous ingestion/validation/routing hot path (core_api_gateway, normalizer_router, schema_registry_service, webhook_adapter_service) are implemented in Go using a shared hexagonal architecture (Collector/Normalizer ports). classifier_agent_service is implemented in Python and interacts with the rest of the system only asynchronously via NATS JetStream (consuming quarantine stream) and via the Schema Registry's HTTP API (submitting proposals) — never directly on the ingestion hot path.
adrs.rationale: Go gives predictable low-latency, low-memory-footprint services that are easy to operate as a small number of binaries/containers, and its concurrency model suits high-throughput stream consumers. Python is kept firmly at the edge of the system (async, best-effort, human-reviewed output) so its slower startup, GIL constraints, and heavier runtime never sit in the request path for producers.
consequences: Two language toolchains/CI pipelines must be maintained (Go + Python) instead of one.
Clear service boundary: classifier_agent_service can be scaled, restarted, or even temporarily down without affecting ingestion of known-shape events.
Go developers must expose stable, versioned HTTP/NATS contracts for the Python service to consume, requiring disciplined API/schema versioning.
Future classifier improvements (e.g. swapping LLM providers, adding local Ollama fallback) are isolated to one service and don't risk destabilizing the core ingestion path.

adrs.title: NATS JetStream as the durable buffer and quarantine mechanism between ingestion and normalization
adrs.context: Ingestion producers (agents, webhooks, OTLP clients) must never be blocked or fail because a downstream store (Loki/Tempo/Mimir/Postgres) is slow or a schema is unrecognized. We need a durable, replayable buffer that decouples 'accept event' from 'validate and route event', and that supports a distinct quarantine path for unknown-shape events that can later be replayed once a schema is approved.
adrs.decision: core_api_gateway and webhook_adapter_service publish all accepted events to NATS JetStream immediately after light validation (auth, envelope shape). normalizer_router consumes the main stream, validates against schema_registry_service, and routes known events to Loki/Tempo/Mimir/Postgres. Unknown-shape events are published to a dedicated quarantine stream/subject, consumed by classifier_agent_service, and replayed back through normalizer_router once schema_registry_service approves a proposal.
adrs.rationale: JetStream is a single self-hostable binary with sufficient durability guarantees for this use case (some data loss tolerance is acceptable per product requirements), avoiding the operational overhead of Kafka while still providing at-least-once delivery, replay, and multiple consumer groups (normalizer, classifier, replay) off the same log.
consequences: Ingestion latency for producers is decoupled from storage backend health — gateway can ack quickly once JetStream accepts the message.
Requires operating and monitoring a JetStream cluster (or single node for dev) as new critical infrastructure; JetStream unavailability stalls the entire pipeline.
Quarantine replay logic in normalizer_router must be idempotent, since replayed events plus newly-approved schema versions can interact with already-processed data.
Some data loss is explicitly accepted as a tradeoff for operational simplicity; this must be communicated to SOAR/compliance stakeholders as a known limitation.

adrs.title: Git-backed YAML/JSON Schema registry with human-approval gate, owned by a dedicated service
adrs.context: The product's core differentiator is that unknown data shapes are never silently dropped or auto-mutated into the ingestion contract; a human must approve any schema change. This requires a system of record for schemas that is versioned, diffable, auditable, and reversible, plus an approval workflow API that both the dashboard (for humans) and classifier_agent_service (for proposals) can use, and that normalizer_router can query cheaply for every event.
adrs.decision: schema_registry_service owns the canonical schema state, persisted as git-backed YAML/JSON Schema files (one commit per approved change) with Postgres used for fast-lookup indexes, proposal metadata, approval audit trail, and agent registry records. classifier_agent_service submits proposals via schema_registry_service's API only; it never writes directly to git or Postgres. normalizer_router calls schema_registry_service (with local caching) for validation lookups rather than reading git directly.
adrs.rationale: Git provides a free, well-understood audit trail (who changed what schema, when, diffable) satisfying compliance/security review needs, while Postgres provides the fast structured queries needed on the hot path (current version lookup, proposal status) that git alone can't serve efficiently. Centralizing ownership in one service avoids split-brain writes to the schema state from multiple services.
consequences: schema_registry_service becomes a critical dependency for normalizer_router; its availability and read latency directly affect ingestion validation throughput, requiring caching/fallback-to-last-known-schema strategies.
Every schema change is fully auditable and revertible via git history, supporting SOAR/compliance review requirements.
Postgres and git can drift if not kept transactionally consistent; schema_registry_service must implement a reliable dual-write (or git-as-source-of-truth-with-Postgres-rebuild) pattern.
Approval UI (dashboard) is decoupled from storage internals — it only talks to schema_registry_service's proposal/approval API.

adrs.title: Dual authentication model: per-agent API keys/JWT for machine traffic, OIDC for human dashboard access
adrs.context: Signal Yard has two very different classes of caller: autonomous agents/webhooks (SOAR tools, dev agents, PM systems, marble-jar) that self-onboard via /start-here-agents and need lightweight, revocable machine credentials; and humans (security, execs, engineers) who need to log into the approval dashboard and Grafana with identity, roles, and SSO support.
adrs.decision: core_api_gateway issues and enforces per-agent API keys (HEC-style token auth) and/or short-lived JWTs for all machine traffic on /v1/collect, OTLP endpoints, webhook adapters, and MCP tool calls. A separate OIDC provider (Keycloak or Dex) is used for human login to the React dashboard and Grafana, with role-based access controls distinguishing viewers, approvers, and admins.
adrs.rationale: Machine and human auth have fundamentally different lifecycle, rotation, and UX requirements; forcing agents through an interactive OIDC flow would block the self-onboarding promise of /start-here-agents, while using static API keys for humans would be insecure and hard to audit. Separating the two lets each be optimized and rotated independently.
consequences: core_api_gateway must implement and maintain its own API key/JWT issuance, storage (hashed), and revocation logic, distinct from OIDC token validation used for dashboard routes.
Two auth systems must be documented clearly in /start-here-agents so new agents aren't confused about which flow applies to them.
Approval actions in the dashboard (schema approve/reject) can be tied to a specific human OIDC identity for audit purposes, satisfying the 'human keeps the veto' requirement.
Requires operating an OIDC provider (Keycloak/Dex) as additional infrastructure alongside the core Go services.

adrs.title: Adopt OTel-native backbones (Loki, Tempo, Mimir/Prometheus) as storage instead of a bespoke event store
adrs.context: Log-shaped, trace-shaped, and metric-shaped signals from heterogeneous agents (dev agent traces, SOAR alerts, PM ticket updates) need durable, queryable storage with good visualization tooling, without the team building and maintaining a custom time-series or log storage engine.
adrs.decision: normalizer_router routes known-shape events by signal type: log-shaped events to Loki, trace-shaped events (e.g. agentic coding runs) to Tempo, metric-shaped events to Mimir/Prometheus, and structured entities (schema registry metadata, agent registry, approval records, SOAR/PM structured records) to PostgreSQL. Grafana is used as the sole visualization layer over all three observability backends plus Postgres data sources.
adrs.rationale: Building on OTLP/Loki-push/Prometheus-remote-write standards means any agent that already emits OpenTelemetry data gets free interoperability with zero custom ingestion code, and Grafana's ecosystem provides proven dashboarding, alerting, and query tooling (LogQL, TraceQL, PromQL) rather than requiring Signal Yard to build its own UI for every signal type.
consequences: Signal Yard's data model is constrained to what fits log/trace/metric paradigms; genuinely relational/structured data (e.g. PM ticket state, approval history) must go to Postgres and be joined manually if cross-referenced with observability data.
Operating four storage backends (Loki, Tempo, Mimir, Postgres) increases infra footprint versus a single database, requiring the docker-compose/Helm stack to manage all of them.
Dashboard team can reuse existing Grafana panels/plugins instead of building custom charting, accelerating delivery of SOAR posture, agent activity, and exec rollup views.
normalizer_router's routing logic must correctly classify signal type per schema entry, making the schema registry's category-to-backend mapping a critical piece of correctness.

architecture.system_diagram_description: External producers (SOAR tools, dev coding agents, PM systems, marble-jar webhooks, generic MCP-native agents) connect to two Go entry-point services: core_api_gateway (handling /start-here-agents onboarding, /v1/collect, OTLP passthrough, and MCP tool endpoints, with machine auth via API key/JWT) and webhook_adapter_service (dedicated receivers for GitHub, Jira, PagerDuty, marble-jar that normalize payloads into the common event envelope). Both publish accepted events into NATS JetStream, which fans out into two logical streams: a main ingestion stream and a quarantine stream. normalizer_router consumes the main stream, calls schema_registry_service to validate each event's shape against the current registry, and routes validated events to one of four storage backends based on signal type: Loki (logs), Tempo (traces), Mimir/Prometheus (metrics), or PostgreSQL (structured entities). Events with unrecognized shapes are instead routed to the quarantine stream, consumed by classifier_agent_service (Python), which calls an LLM provider (Anthropic/OpenAI or local Ollama) to infer a category and field mapping, then submits a structured schema patch proposal (JSON Schema + routing YAML diff) to schema_registry_service's proposals API. schema_registry_service persists approved schemas as git-backed YAML/JSON Schema files plus fast-lookup metadata in PostgreSQL, and exposes a review/approve API. A human-facing React + TypeScript dashboard (using shadcn/ui and TanStack Query) authenticates users via OIDC (Keycloak/Dex) and calls schema_registry_service to display proposal diffs for human approval/rejection; upon approval, normalizer_router replays previously quarantined events for that shape through the now-updated schema. The same dashboard embeds Grafana, which reads directly from Loki, Tempo, Mimir/Prometheus, and PostgreSQL to render pre-built dashboards (SOAR posture, agent activity heatmap, dev-agent productivity, exec rollup). All services and infra (Go services, Postgres, NATS JetStream, Loki, Tempo, Mimir, Grafana) run together via docker-compose in dev and via a Helm chart in multi-node production deployments.

infrastructure.deployment_target: Kubernetes (Helm chart) for production, docker-compose for local/dev
suggested_managed_services: Managed PostgreSQL (RDS/Cloud SQL/Azure Database for PostgreSQL)
Managed NATS JetStream (Synadia Cloud) or self-hosted StatefulSet
Grafana Cloud (Loki/Tempo/Mimir) or self-hosted Grafana stack
Managed Keycloak/Dex (OIDC) via container or managed IdP integration
Object storage (S3/GCS) for Loki/Tempo/Mimir chunk backends
Managed secrets store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Kubernetes Sealed Secrets)
Git hosting (GitHub/GitLab) with webhook-based CI for schema registry Git source of truth
infrastructure.scaling_notes: Go services (core_api_gateway, normalizer_router, schema_registry_service, webhook_adapter_service) are stateless and horizontally scalable behind a k8s Deployment/HPA based on CPU and NATS consumer lag. classifier_agent_service (Python) should scale independently with HPA tuned to queue depth/latency since LLM calls are the bottleneck; consider a separate node pool with higher memory/GPU if using local Ollama models. NATS JetStream needs a dedicated StatefulSet with persistent volumes and replica count >=3 for durability. PostgreSQL should be vertically scaled first, with read replicas for Grafana/dashboard queries. Loki/Tempo/Mimir benefit from object-storage-backed scalable mode for high retention/query load. Schema registry Git operations should be rate-limited/queued to avoid Git contention under high approval throughput.
